questions.q: Which of the following attributes does a population have that an individual organism does not?
questions.solution: A population has certain attributes whereas an individual organism does not. An individual may have births and deaths, <mark>but a population has birth rates and death rates.</mark> In a population these rates refer to per capita births and deaths. The rates, hence, expressed are change in numbers (increase or decrease) with respect to members of the population. Here is an example. If in a pond there were 20 lotus plants last year and through reproduction 8 new plants are added, taking the current population to 28, we calculate the birth rate as 8/20 = 0.4 offspring per locus per year. If 4 individuals in a laboratory population of 40 fruit flies died during a specified time interval, say a week, the death rate in the population during that period is 4/40 = 0.1 individuals per fruit fly per week

questions.q: What is a factor that causes changes in the population size over time?
questions.solution: The size of a population for any species is not a static parameter<mark>. It keeps changing with time, depending on various factors including food availability,</mark> predation pressure and adverse weather. In fact, it is these changes in population density that give us some idea of what is happening to the population – whether it is flourishing or declining. Whatever might be the ultimate reasons, the density of a population in a given habitat during a given period, fluctuates due to changes in four basic processes. Natality and immigration contribute to an increase in population density and mortality and emigration to a decrease. (i) Natality refers to the number of births during a given period in the population that are added to the initial density. (ii) Mortality is the number of deaths in the population during a given period. (iii) Immigration is the number of individuals of the same species that have come into the habitat from elsewhere during the time period under consideration. (iv)Emigration is the number of individuals of the population who left the habitat and gone elsewhere during the time period under consideration.

questions.q: What do populations evolve to maximize in their habitat?
questions.solution: <mark>Populations evolve to maximize their reproductive fitness, also called Darwinian fitness (high r value)</mark>, in the habitat in which they live. So, which is desirable for maximizing fitness? questions.solution: Populations evolve to maximize their reproductive fitness, also called Darwinian fitness (high r value), in the habitat in which they live. Under a particular set of selection pressures, organisms evolve towards the most efficient reproductive strategy. Some organisms breed only once in their lifetime (Pacific salmon fish, bamboo) while others breed many times during their lifetime (most birds and mammals<mark>). Some produce a large number of small-sized offspring (Oysters, pelagic fishes)</mark> while others produce a small number of large-sized offspring (birds, mammals). So, which is desirable for maximizing fitness? Ecologists suggest that life history traits of organisms have evolved in relation to the constraints imposed by the abiotic and biotic components of the habitat in which they live. Evolution of life history traits in different species is currently an important area of research being conducted by ecologists.

questions.q: How are interspecific interactions described in terms of their effects on species?
options: They are always harmful to both species involved
They are either beneficial, detrimental, or neutral to one or both species
They only have beneficial effects on one species
They result in complete isolation of the species involved
questions.solution: Even in minimal communities, many interactive linkages exist, although all may not be readily apparent. Interspecific interactions arise from the interaction of populations of two different species. <mark>They could be beneficial, detrimental or neutral (neither harm nor benefit) to one of the species or both</mark>. Assigning a ‘+’ sign for beneficial interaction, ‘-’ sign for detrimental and 0 for neutral interaction.Both the species benefit in mutualism and both lose in competition in their interactions with each other. In both parasitism and predation only one species benefits (parasite and predator, respectively) and the interaction is detrimental to the other species (host and prey, respectively). The interaction where one species is benefitted and the other is neither benefited or harmed is called commensalism. In amensalism on the other hand one species is harmed whereas the other is unaffected. Predation, parasitism and commensalism share a common characteristic– the interacting species live closely together. Therefore, competition is best defined as a process in which the fitness of one species (measured in terms of its ‘r’ the intrinsic rate of increase) is significantly lower in the presence of another species. It is relatively easy to demonstrate in laboratory experiments, as Gause and other experimental ecologists did, when resources are limited the competitively superior species will eventually eliminate the other species, but evidence for such competitive exclusion occurring in nature is not always conclusive.

questions.q: What percentage of all insects are known to be phytophagous?
questions.solution: For plants, herbivores are the predators. <mark>Nearly 25 percent of all insects are known to be phytophagous (feeding on plant sap and other parts of plants).</mark> The problem is particularly severe for plants because, unlike animals, they cannot run away from their predators. Plants therefore have evolved an astonishing variety of morphological and chemical defenses against herbivores. Thorns (Acacia, Cactus) are the most common morphological means of defense. Many plants produce and store chemicals that make the herbivore sick when they are eaten, inhibit feeding or digestion, disrupt its reproduction or even kill it. You must have seen the weed Calotropis growing in abandoned fields. The plant produces highly poisonous cardiac glycosides and that is why you never see any cattle or goats browsing on this plant. A wide variety of chemical substances that we extract from plants on a commercial scale (nicotine, caffeine, quinine, strychnine, opium, etc.,) are produced by them actually as defenses against grazers and browsers.

questions.q: What did Darwin believe to be a potent force in organic evolution?
questions.solution: <mark>When Darwin spoke of the struggle for existence and survival of the fittest in nature, he was convinced that <mark>interspecific competition is a potent force in organic evolution</mark>. It is generally believed that competition occurs when closely related species compete for the same resources that are limiting, but this is not entirely true. Firstly, totally unrelated species could also compete for the same resource. For instance, in some shallow South American lakes, visiting flamingoes and resident fishes compete for their common food, the zooplankton in the lake. Secondly, resources need not be limiting for competition to occur; in interference competition, the feeding efficiency of one species might be reduced due to the interfering and inhibitory presence of the other species, even if resources (food and space) are abundant.

A. Mutualism1. Both species benefit
B. Competition2. One species benefits while the other is harmed
C. Parasitism3. One species benefits and the other is unaffected
D. Commensalism4. Both species lose
questions.solution: In mutualism, both species benefit. Competition results in both species losing. Parasitism involves one species benefiting while the other is harmed, and in commensalism, one species benefits while the other is unaffected.
questions.subject: Zoology

questions.q:
Predation and Its RolesDescriptions
A. Energy Transfer1. Keeps prey populations under control
B. Control of Prey Populations2. Maintains diversity by reducing competition
C. Biological Control3. Transfers energy from plants to higher trophic levels
D. Species Diversity4. Involves using predators to manage agricultural pests
questions.solution: Predation transfers energy fixed by plants to higher trophic levels. It also keeps prey populations under control, is used in biological control methods, and helps maintain species diversity by reducing competition among prey.
questions.subject: Zoology

questions.q:
Defenses Against PredationExamples
A. Camouflage1. Thorns like those in Acacia and Cactus
B. Poison2. Special chemicals that make the plant or insect distasteful
C. Thorns3. Color patterns that make the organism blend into its environment
D. Chemical Defenses4. Substances that disrupt digestion or reproduction of herbivores
questions.solution: Camouflage involves color patterns that blend an organism into its environment. Poison is a chemical defense making organisms distasteful. Thorns are physical defenses like those in Acacia and Cactus. Chemical defenses include substances that affect herbivores’ digestion or reproduction.
questions.subject: Zoology

questions.q:
Ecological InteractionsInteraction Effects
A. Interspecific Interaction1. Interaction between different species
B. Mutualism2. One species benefits and the other is harmed
C. Parasitism3. One species benefits while the other is unaffected
D. Amensalism4. Both species benefit from the interaction
questions.solution: Interspecific interaction involves interactions between different species. Mutualism results in both species benefiting. Parasitism benefits one species while harming the other, and amensalism involves one species being harmed while the other is unaffected.
questions.subject: Zoology

questions.q:
Examples of PredationPredation Context
A. Tiger and Deer1. Controls invertebrate species diversity in intertidal zones
B. Sparrow and Seed2. A predator consuming seeds
C. Starfish Pisaster3. Maintains energy transfer and ecosystem stability
D. Monarch Butterfly4. Acquires chemical defenses during caterpillar stage
questions.solution: The tiger and deer represent energy transfer and ecosystem stability. The sparrow eating seeds is an example of a predator consuming seeds. The starfish Pisaster controls species diversity in intertidal zones, and the Monarch butterfly acquires chemical defenses during its caterpillar stage.
questions.subject: Zoology

questions.q:
Ecological ConceptsEffects
A. Herbivory1. Plants develop chemicals to deter herbivores
B. Invasive Species2. Species introduced without natural predators can spread rapidly
C. Chemical Defenses3. Animals that feed on plants
D. Predator Efficiency4. Overexploitation of prey can lead to predator extinction
questions.solution: Herbivory involves animals that feed on plants. Invasive species can spread rapidly if introduced without natural predators. Plants develop chemical defenses to deter herbivores, and too efficient predators can lead to their own extinction due to overexploitation of prey.
questions.subject: Zoology

questions.q:
Competition ContextsExamples
A. Interference Competition1. Flamingoes and fishes competing for zooplankton
B. Resource Limitation2. Abingdon tortoise extinction due to goats
C. Competitive Exclusion3. Species expanding distribution when competing species is removed
D. Competitive Release4. Feeding efficiency reduced by the presence of another species
questions.solution: Interference competition occurs when one species' feeding efficiency is reduced by the presence of another species. Resource limitation involves competition for limited resources, as seen with flamingoes and fishes. Competitive exclusion is demonstrated by the Abingdon tortoise's extinction due to goats. Competitive release is shown by a species expanding its range when a competing species is removed.
questions.subject: Zoology

questions.q:
Definitions of CompetitionCharacteristics
A. Interspecific Competition1. Two closely related species cannot co-exist indefinitely
B. Interference Competition2. Fitness of one species is lower in the presence of another
C. Competitive Exclusion Principle3. Competition can occur even if resources are abundant
D. Resource Partitioning4. Species avoid competition by using resources differently
questions.solution: Interspecific competition is where the fitness of one species is lowered in the presence of another. Interference competition can occur even if resources are abundant. The Competitive Exclusion Principle states that closely related species cannot co-exist indefinitely. Resource partitioning is when species use resources differently to avoid competition.
questions.subject: Zoology

questions.q:
Ecological ExperimentsFindings
A. Gause’s Experiments1. Balanus excludes Chathamalus from the intertidal zone
B. Connell’s Field Experiments2. Five warbler species co-exist due to different foraging patterns
C. MacArthur’s Study3. Competitive exclusion observed with limited resources
D. Abingdon Tortoise Case4. Tortoise extinction due to goat browsing efficiency
questions.solution: Gause’s experiments showed competitive exclusion with limited resources. Connell’s field experiments demonstrated Balanus excluding Chathamalus. MacArthur’s study showed five warbler species co-existing due to different foraging patterns. The Abingdon tortoise case involved extinction due to goat browsing efficiency.
questions.subject: Zoology

questions.q:
Concepts in CompetitionDescriptions
A. Struggle for Existence1. Lower fitness due to presence of another species
B. Fitness Measure2. Theory that closely related species cannot co-exist indefinitely
C. Competitive Exclusion3. Related and unrelated species competing for resources
D. Co-existence Mechanisms4. Avoidance of competition by different resource use
questions.solution: The struggle for existence involves both related and unrelated species competing for resources. Fitness measure refers to lower fitness due to the presence of another species. Competitive exclusion is the theory that closely related species cannot co-exist indefinitely. Co-existence mechanisms involve avoiding competition by using resources differently.
questions.subject: Zoology

questions.q:
Parasite EvolutionEvolutionary Features
A. Host-Specific Parasites1. Mechanisms to counteract host defenses
B. Co-evolution of Parasites2. Loss of unnecessary sense organs
C. Parasitic Adaptations3. Parasites that can parasitize only one species
D. Intermediate Hosts4. Facilitates parasitisation of the primary host
questions.solution: Host-specific parasites can parasitize only a single species, and co-evolution involves mechanisms to counteract host defenses. Parasitic adaptations include the loss of unnecessary sense organs. Intermediate hosts facilitate parasitisation of the primary host.
questions.subject: Zoology

questions.q:
Parasitic LifestyleCharacteristics
A. Parasitic Plants1. Lives on the external surface of the host
B. Ectoparasites2. Derives nutrition from the host plant
C. Endoparasites3. Eggs resemble the host’s eggs
D. Brood Parasites4. Lives inside the host’s body
questions.solution: Parasitic plants, like Cuscuta, derive nutrition from the host plant. Ectoparasites live on the external surface of the host. Endoparasites live inside the host's body. Brood parasites lay eggs that resemble the host’s eggs.
questions.subject: Zoology

questions.q:
Parasitic AdaptationsExamples
A. Loss of Sense Organs1. Clinging onto the host
B. Adhesive Organs2. Increased production of offspring
C. High Reproductive Capacity3. No need to locate food independently
D. Loss of Digestive System4. Reduced reliance on the host’s environment
questions.solution: Loss of sense organs in parasites means they do not need to locate food independently. Adhesive organs help in clinging onto the host. High reproductive capacity ensures the production of more offspring. The loss of the digestive system reduces reliance on the host's environment for digestion.
questions.subject: Zoology

questions.q:
Parasitic RelationshipsExamples
A. Host-Specific Parasite1. Lice on humans
B. Generalist Parasite2. Cuckoo laying eggs in a crow’s nest
C. Co-evolution3. Parasites that can parasitize multiple hosts
D. Brood Parasitism4. Host and parasite evolving together
questions.solution: Host-specific parasites, like lice on humans, parasitize only one species. Generalist parasites can parasitize multiple hosts. Co-evolution involves both the host and the parasite evolving together. Brood parasitism is exemplified by the cuckoo laying eggs in a crow’s nest.
questions.subject: Zoology

questions.q:
Commensalism ExamplesBeneficiary Species
A. Orchid on Mango Branch1. Orchid
B. Barnacles on Whale2. Barnacles
C. Cattle Egret3. Clown Fish
D. Clown Fish4. Cattle Egret
questions.solution: In commensalism, the orchid benefits by growing on the mango branch, the barnacles benefit by growing on the whale, the cattle egret benefits from insects stirred up by grazing cattle, and the clown fish benefits from the protection offered by the sea anemone.
questions.subject: Zoology

questions.q:
Mutualism ExamplesInteraction Types
A. Lichens1. Fungus and Algae/Cyanobacteria
B. Mycorrhizae2. Fungi and Plant Roots
C. Fig Tree and Wasp3. Pollination
D. Orchid and Bee4. Seed Dispersal
questions.solution: Lichens represent a mutualistic relationship between fungus and algae/cyanobacteria, mycorrhizae involve mutualism between fungi and plant roots, fig trees and wasps engage in mutualistic pollination, and orchids attract bees for pollination.
questions.subject: Zoology

questions.q:
Mutualistic Plant-Animal RelationshipsBenefits to Plant
A. Fig Tree1. Pollination by Bee
B. Orchid2. Pollination by Wasp
C. Higher Plants3. Nutrient Absorption
D. Lichens4. Photosynthesis
questions.solution: Fig trees benefit from pollination by wasps, orchids benefit from pollination by bees, higher plants benefit from nutrient absorption facilitated by mycorrhizae, and lichens benefit from photosynthesis by algae/cyanobacteria.
questions.subject: Zoology

questions.q:
Evolutionary RelationshipConsequences
A. Co-evolution of Fig and Wasp1. Orchid Fails to Attract Bee
B. Sexual Deceit in Orchid2. Wasp Pollinates Fig
C. Lack of Co-evolution3. Orchid Attracts Bee
D. Mutualism Breakdown4. Lack of Mutual Benefits
questions.solution: Co-evolution between fig trees and wasps results in successful pollination. Sexual deceit in orchids ensures bee attraction. A lack of co-evolution can lead to failure in attracting pollinators. Breakdown of mutualism results in a lack of mutual benefits.
questions.subject: Zoology

questions.q:
Challenges in MutualismConsequences
A. Change in Pollinator Behavior1. Failure in Pollination
B. Evolutionary Mismatch2. Mutualism Breakdown
C. Presence of Cheaters3. Loss of mutual benefits
D. Breakdown of Mutualism4. Pollinator Cheats Without Helping Plant
questions.solution: A change in pollinator behavior can lead to failure in pollination. Evolutionary mismatches may cause mutualism breakdown. The presence of cheaters results in the pollinator benefiting without aiding the plant, and the breakdown of mutualism leads to the loss of mutual benefits.
questions.subject: Zoology

B. Barnacles on Whale2. Whale
C. Cattle Egret with Grazing Cattle3. Sea Anemone
D. Clownfish with Sea Anemone4. Cattle
